captions.text: Diorite resists the chisel; that is the point. A ruler of Lagash chose a stone that would not wear, and the crisp edge of the brow has held for four thousand years.
Cast after the limestone bust found in the sculptor Thutmose's workshop at Amarna. Only one eye is inlaid — quartz set with wax. Circle to her left and the gaze switches off.
A lioness's head on a woman's body, worked small in glazed faience. Sekhmet's scale here is domestic — power kept close at hand rather than enthroned.
The raised arm is caught mid-address, the breastplate crowded with narrative, the feet bare. Below the knee, a small Cupid on a dolphin does the quiet structural work of holding up the emperor.
No diadem, no theatrics: a soldier-emperor's plain fringe combed forward over the forehead, cut in Carrara marble. Second-century power, dressed down on purpose.
Michelangelo's Moses for the tomb of Julius II, here in plaster: the horns, the tablets clamped under one arm, and a right hand pulling the beard aside as the seated body turns to rise.
Iron, brass, tin, arrows, cowries — each insertion driven in by the nganga who activated the figure, sealing an oath or a dispute. Walk around it; the accumulation has no front.
The carved head is finished; the torso disappears into a bound package of cloth and organic matter. This sculpture is a container first — what it holds outranks what it shows.
Cottonwood carved, then built up: pigment, cotton cloth, tanned leather, metal. The ogre's authority is assembled from additions — turn it slowly and count the separate decisions.
Late sixth-century brass. Rays spike from the single halo that frames head and body together — the "combined" of the title. Rake the light across the metal and it does the announcing itself.

power-and-presence.invitation: Every figure in this room was made to outrank you. Rulers in stone that resists the chisel, a queen with one seeing eye, guardians bristling with driven iron — each is a claim to authority staged in material. Stand where their makers never intended: close, at eye level, on every side.
power-and-presence.coda: Authority, it turns out, is a made thing — a stone chosen, a nail driven, an arm raised to the right height. You have just seen it from angles it was never built to allow.

sacred-forms.invitation: None of the objects in this room was made to be looked at the way you are about to look at it. They are instruments of address — a door for a dead priest, a stand raised for ritual, a robe carrying doctrine, a mask meant to be danced — built to work between people and what they worshipped. The museum holds them still; here, you may turn them.
sacred-forms.coda: These forms once faced gods, spirits, and the dead; for the last few minutes they faced you. Their work was never display.

captions.text: The falcon towers; the king stands no taller than its legs. Note how the metagraywacke holds one continuous polish across both bodies, binding god and pharaoh in a single dark stone.

Not a door that opens: a limestone threshold for the priest Iryenakhet, cut so the dead could come through to receive offerings. Stand square in front — this face was carved for exactly that position.
The robe is the sermon: carved realms of desire cross chest, shoulders, and back. Turn the figure slowly — the imagery continues where a gallery wall would stop you.
A Goryeo-period bodhisattva of compassion in gilt wood, set with copper, iron, and crystal. Rake the light low across the gilding and find the inlays by their answering flash.
Javanese carvers cut this from andesite, a volcanic stone whose pocked grain keeps its tool marks. Look for the join between elephant head and human body — the seam that is not there.

Carved around 1000 CE from guaiacum, a wood dense enough to sink in water, with shell set into the dark surface. The figure is support in the strictest sense: its purpose is the stand it offers upward.
Carved to be worn on top of the head, not over the face. Tip it and look up into the hollow — the fitting for a dancer's crown, a view no vitrine allows.
Wood, glass, beads, brass tacks, pigment — each material doing separate work on one carved body. Find the junction where the mother's arm meets the child; the composition is braced around it.
A cast after the marble Michelangelo finished before turning twenty-five — the only work he ever signed, on the strap across Mary's chest. Walk behind; in St. Peter's, the chapel forbids it.
Donatello set the saint on spread legs behind his grounded shield, weight forward, chin lifted — a soldier in the instant before. The stance was made to read from the street below the niche.

the-work-of-the-surface.invitation: Sculpture is supposed to be about mass. Everything decisive here happens within millimeters of it — a lion hunt cut shallow into alabaster, a cosmos incised on a robe, a court painted over glaze. Watch the skin of things work.
the-work-of-the-surface.coda: Depth was never the point. A few worked millimeters proved enough to carry a hunt, a cosmos, and a court out of their centuries and into this room.

captions.text: A royal hunt held in a few millimeters of gypsum alabaster, from the Northwest Palace at Nimrud. Rake the light low across the slab and watch the shallow cutting separate rein, bowstring, and mane.
Carved by a Kongo artist in 1861, the relief takes its path from the ivory itself, following the tusk's taper and curve — no single viewpoint contains it.
A surface taken from a surface: Charles Carpeaux's 1904 plaster carries the Bayon's twelfth-to-thirteenth-century naval battle at one remove, oars and hulls passed intact through the mold.
Look past the figure to what it wears. The Northern Qi carver treated the robe as a picture plane, working the realms of desire into limestone drapery.
Michelangelo, still in his teens, graded emergence itself: some combatants stand nearly free of the marble while others stay half-drowned in it, beneath a top edge left rough with tool marks.
One disc of marble, several depths of finish. The Virgin's head rises almost into the round and past the rim; behind her, figures thin to little more than drawing.
Container and creature share a single clay skin. The Quapaw maker shaped the vessel as the Underwater Panther itself, a being of Mississippian belief, so the hollow sits inside the animal's body.
Late Shang bronze, its ornament worked in negative: every ridge on this wine vessel was first cut into a mold, and the poured metal only remembers the pattern.
Four faces, no back — a head that fronts every direction at once. Turn it slowly; with each quarter revolution a new face takes the place of the one you just left.
Overglaze polychromy and gold lay a courtly gathering onto stonepaste. The picture accepts a curved ground, its figures bending with the bowl's profile.

bodies-in-motion.invitation: Nothing in this room moves, and everything is mid-act: a disc at the top of its arc, a hold about to break, a stride that never lands. Each sculptor chose a single instant and built the before and after into it. Turn the works as you go — the instant reads differently from every side.
bodies-in-motion.coda: The works stay exactly where you left them — mid-throw, mid-fall, mid-step. Whatever completed the motion, you brought it with you.

captions.text: The bronze is lost; the coil survives. One arc runs from the trailing toes through the twisted torso to the raised disc. The head is a modern restoration — circle the figure and judge whether it turns the right way.
Two bodies resolve into one knot of marble. Drop your view to mat level: the lower figure's arm is barred behind his back, and every contact point — knee, hip, grip — carries transferred weight.
Held in the Saint-Raymond reserves, this small terracotta is usually out of public view. Fired clay keeps the swing of a step at statuette scale — lean in closer than any vitrine would allow.

Carved for the tomb of Julius II, though the bonds barely register: a thin band across the chest, one arm folded overhead. The pose sits nearer to sleep than struggle — motion caught at the point of release.

Its companion resists: arms lashed behind, torso twisting off its axis, head wrenched aside. This plaster cast records the marble's worked surface — rake the light low across it to find the tool marks.

Father and sons on one rising diagonal, the serpents supplying every connection between the three bodies. Step around behind — a view the frontal composition never planned for — and follow each coil to its anchor.
No head, no arms — Rodin kept only what walking requires. Both feet press flat to the ground at once, a stance no mid-stride body holds; the motion is assembled, not observed.
One figure from Le Jeu de l'écharpe, the Sèvres table centerpiece — an object made to be seen from every side. Unglazed biscuit porcelain keeps the surface matte; the scarf carries the motion.

Cut for the tapering corner of the Aphaia temple's west pediment, the warrior folds to fit the gable: propped on one elbow, legs stretched into the angle. He was made to be read from far below — try that view.
Washington lists her not on view; here she never leaves the floor. Eberle pitches the child's weight well past her feet — a pose that only works because momentum, not balance, is holding her up.

A fighter misnamed a gladiator: the lunge stretches him along one line from rear heel to raised left arm, gaze lifted toward a mounted opponent long gone. Sight down that line from behind the back foot.

what-survives.invitation: Little in this room is whole, and none of it apologizes. Most of these works were edited by accident down to the part that could outlast its circumstances. Read the breaks as closely as the surfaces: the fracture is the most recent carving.
what-survives.coda: These works were made once by hand and a second time by loss. After this room, every intact statue you meet is a fragment that hasn't happened yet.

captions.text: A seated hero — Ajax, perhaps — reduced to trunk and thighs, yet the twist between hip and ribcage still carries the whole intention. Circle it: the pose resolves only in the round. Michelangelo studied it closely.
No name, no date, no head or arms: a young body known only by its skin. Notice how lightly the musculature is stated — a frame caught in the interval before definition.
Phidias's gold-and-ivory colossus is wholly gone; this plaster records a copy kept in the library of Athena's sanctuary at Pergamon — survival at two removes from a vanished original.
One of the horses that hauled the moon's chariot, worked past exhaustion: jaw strained, a vein rising along the muzzle. In the east pediment it sank at the corner; here you can meet it from below.
A head carved in oak in 1430 to be exactly this: the Baptist's head on a platter. Alone in this room, its fragmentary form is the sculptor's subject, not time's edit.
From the palace walls of Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud: an eagle-headed demon, wing feathers incised row by row into alabaster. Its edges are breaks, not borders — the wall it belonged to kept going.
The resting Hercules of this type leans his whole colossal fatigue on a club; this head arrives without one, its downcast gaze still presupposing a body below.
A casualty from the north side of the Pergamon Altar's battle of gods and giants. The hair is cut with deep drill channels — where light rakes across them, shadow does half the modelling.
A horse's head in bronze from Herculaneum, ending at the neck. Look into the opening: the casting is hollow, the metal only a skin — large bronzes were always shells.

A daughter of Akhenaten in quartzite from Tell el-Amarna, the skull drawn long in the Amarna manner. The elongated crown is design; the absent body, loss — the whole room turns on telling the two apart.

newExhibition.title: The Other Kingdom
newExhibition.summary: Sculptors have almost never carved animals as mere animals. Across three thousand years and six cultures, these twelve works show the beast recruited as god, trophy, guardian, vessel — and finally, a ride.
newExhibition.invitation: Begin with vessels that pour through animal bodies; end at the fairground. Ask of each creature the only question that matters here: what job was it given? And turn everything — several of these works were made to be circled, worn, or ridden, and the screen permits what the gallery rope would not.
newExhibition.coda: The oldest animal in this room poured wine; the newest carried children. In between, the beast did whatever we could not manage for ourselves — guarded, warned, mourned, and stood for gods.

works.text: A feline and a snake share one ceramic body, three thousand years old. Circle it to find where the animal ends and the stirrup-shaped spout begins — the join is the potter's whole argument.
Shang casters crowded this bronze wine ewer with masks, dragons, and animals that actually exist. Rake the light low across the surface and sort the real creatures from the invented ones.
A keeper lifts the cage door and the lion is already at speed. Carved for Ashurbanipal's palace at Nineveh, where the royal hunt was staged and only one side knew the ending.
The she-wolf turns her head to face whoever approaches, teats heavy, twins feeding beneath. Look for the seam in time: the bronze wolf and the plump children were made centuries apart.

One of the horses that hauled Selene's moon-chariot across the Parthenon's east pediment, done in: eye bulging, nostril flared, jaw slack. It sank below the pediment floor; here you may finally meet its eye.
Apis was a living bull, chosen by priests at Memphis and mourned like a king when it died. This one is serpentinite — turn it and notice how little light the dark stone concedes.

This lion guarded the temple of Al-Lat at Palmyra, a gazelle sheltered between its forepaws. Smashed in 2015 and rebuilt the same year as digital geometry — a guardian that outlasted its own limestone.
Half panther, half person, kneeling with forepaws on thighs. Wood rarely survives the centuries; this small Florida carving did, and every cut still reads as deliberate.
A guardian from the Bayon at Angkor, more architecture than anatomy: squared chest, locked haunches, a face flattened toward mask. Walk behind it — these figures were carved to be passed, not faced.
The Underwater Panther, a being said to live beneath rivers, arrives as the thing it haunted: a vessel for holding water. Quapaw hands shaped it around 1500, in clay and pigment.
A ram built to be worn: horns curling back above openings cut for a dancer's eyes. Look underneath, where a mount now does the work a moving human head once did.

The only animal here built to carry us: a carousel horse of about 1917, basswood and paint with glass eyes and steel fittings. Outside-row horses faced the paying crowd, so one flank got the carver's best attention.

pairings.title: Gods in Mid-Arc
pairings.line: Two gods stopped at the top of the swing — one arm cocked to hurl, one leg lifted inside the wheel of the dance — fifteen centuries between throws.

pairings.title: Carved by the Victor
pairings.line: Two defeated warriors sink onto a single supporting arm, each carved in marble by the civilization that defeated him, two thousand years apart.

pairings.title: Neolithic Contemporaries
pairings.line: Rough contemporaries at opposite ends of Eurasia: Aegean marble pares the female body to flat planes while Jomon clay swells it into ridged ornament.

pairings.title: Folded Around Thought
pairings.line: Seven centuries apart, both close the seated body around its own interior — a bronze chin on a knuckled hand, a terracotta torso curling in on itself.

pairings.title: The Official Face
pairings.line: Thirteen centuries apart, two states issue the same argument: authority is a face brought to perfect, untroubled symmetry.

pairings.title: The Work of Holding
pairings.line: An ocean and four centuries apart, each mother steadies a child with the frankness of a load-bearing column, her gaze fixed somewhere past him.
